paper.title: Rate-Resolved Text Evaluation with Masked Diffusion Language Models

author.affiliation: The University of Manchester
University of Pittsburgh
The University of Manchester

paper.abstract: Text evaluation is increasingly driven by scalar judgments from autoregressive likelihoods, prompted judges, and learned evaluators. While effective for ranking systems, scalar scores collapse diverse evaluation behavior into a single dimension. We propose rate-resolved evaluation, a reconstruction-based evaluation paradigm using masked diffusion language models. Masked diffusion models reconstruct text under varying masking rates, naturally exposing how quality signals behave as contextual evidence decreases. We preserve this reconstruction structure as a reconstruction profile: a vector of band-conditioned losses that captures how different quality signals persist or degrade across context regimes. On SummEval, preserving masking-rate structure provides complementary information beyond the scalar baselines tested here, improving fusion with autoregressive likelihood and prompted judges. On WMT MQM zh-en, the same reconstruction process produces different evaluation behaviors at different masking rates, yielding a tunable tradeoff between ranking translation quality and localizing error spans. Our results suggest that, in the tested settings, diffusion reconstruction can expose evaluative structure that is not captured by the scalar baselines we evaluate, through structured recoverability under controlled corruption.

paper.title: Retell, Reward, Repeat: Reinforcement Learning for Narrative Theory-Informed Counterfactual Storytelling

author.affiliation: School of Computer Science and Engineering, UNSW Sydney

paper.abstract: Counterfactual storytelling exposes LLM shortcomings in causal reasoning, where few-shot prompting and SFT fail to produce logical and rational narratives. This case study introduces Retell, Reward, Repeat (RRR), a narrative theory-informed RL pipeline that teaches causal story structure. We extend an existing counterfactual stories dataset with human-annotated stages of narrative equilibrium, synthesising Structuralist Narratology with scalar narrativity. An aligned LLM-as-judge automates this framework to output reward signals, teaching the policy LLM to generate texts with causal narrative structure. Evaluations show that RRR-trained 7/8B LLMs outperform few-shot and SFT baselines in logic, rationality, and completeness, also aligning with a blind human preference subset. RRR offers a linguistically grounded, cost-effective post-training mechanism for LLM storytelling using a small, query-only dataset, showing the value of integrating linguistic theories into contemporary NLP.

paper.abstract: Large language models excel in high-resource languages, but their performance on low-resource languages (LRLs) depends mainly on two factors: limited training data and inefficient tokenization. For non-Latin scripts, tokenizers whose vocabularies are largely English produce high token fertility, that is, they split words into more subword tokens per word, increasing sequence length and computational cost. Vocabulary expansion addresses this by adding language-specific tokens, but the trade-offs it introduces are not fully characterized. We evaluate this strategy across architectures and model scales,1 focusing on two LRLs, Tibetan and Sanskrit. Each new token requires training a new embedding. Our results show that as more tokens are added under limited continued pre-training data, these embeddings remain under-trained. While expansion improves efficiency, performance peaks at small expansion sizes and decreases as the vocabulary grows.

paper.title: A Multi-Stage Agentic Framework for Effective Counter-Narrative Generation and Refinement

author.affiliation: School of Industrial & Intelligent Systems Engineering, Tel Aviv University

paper.abstract: The rapid diffusion of hate speech and misinformation on social networks challenges democratic societies, since direct suppression efforts may deepen polarization, fuel public distrusts, and strengthen extremist narratives. LLM-driven counter-narratives (CNs) offer a promising way to reduce those risks, yet their effectiveness depends on rhetorical and stylistic choices that remain poorly understood. We present a multi-stage agent-based framework for generating, refining, and evaluating CNs, applied to pro-Russian hate and misinformation narratives on the war with Ukraine and adaptable to other domains. A pilot experiment with human evaluators identifies effective technique style pairings, such as repetition with emotional framing enhancing persuasiveness. Building on these insights, we introduce a multi-agent refinement process that iteratively improves CNs for persuasiveness, emotional engagement, and shareability. After human validation confirmed improvement, an automated safety analysis shows that our refined CNs match or improve on expert-written counterspeech. A simulated experiment then shows that they reduce the perceived strength of pro-Russian narratives and consistently outperform a vanilla LLM baseline, highlighting a pathway toward scalable, narrative-specific interventions against hate speech and misinformation. Code and data accompanying this work are publicly available at https://github.com/carmelkron/ inlg2026-counter-narratives.

paper.title: CAI-dLLM: Convergence Aware Inference for Diffusion Language Models

author.affiliation: Virginia Tech
Virginia Tech
Virginia Tech

paper.abstract: Diffusion language models can generate many tokens in parallel, but they still require repeated denoising steps during inference. This makes generation costly, especially when the model continues to recompute tokens that are already stable. To address these limitations, we propose CAI-dLLM, a training-free inference method that uses first-step confidence to guide denoising and reduce inference time. Specifically, CAI-dLLM commits easy tokens earlier, allocates more denoising steps to harder tokens, and adjusts decoding schedules across output blocks. As it relies only on first-step confidence signals, it does not require retraining, extra predictors, or weight updates. We evaluate CAI-dLLM on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct across math, code, reasoning, commonsense, and long-context (Dream-7B). Relative to strong existing caching baselines (DualCache, ES-dLLM), CAI-dLLM gives consistent marginal speedups of 1.7–5.8×, with accuracy at or above no-cache decoding on some tasks (e.g. LLaDA GSM8K: 77.41% vs. 76.27%) and a drop of up to 4.4 points on harder multi-step reasoning tasks (LLaDA BBH). Relative to no-cache decoding, speedups reach up to 44.8× on long chain-of-thought tasks, with energy reduced by up to 95.3%. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/flarebrienne/CAI-DLLM/

paper.title: M^2Preserve: A Multidimensional Framework for Evaluating Meaning Preservation in Text Simplification

author.affiliation: School of Computational and Mathematical Sciences, Cardiff University, UK; Faculty of Computing and Information Technology, King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia
School of Computational and Mathematical Sciences, Cardiff University, UK

paper.abstract: Evaluating meaning preservation in text simplification remains an open challenge: human evaluations rely on coarse-grained holistic judgments, while automatic metrics frequently misalign with human assessments and fail to capture simplification-specific edits. We introduce M2Preserve, a multidimensional fine-grained framework that decomposes meaning preservation into two complementary dimensions, Completeness and Faithfulness, defined over key facts aligned between original and simplified texts. To support evaluation, we construct M2PreserveEval, a paragraph-level dataset with 8,773 human-annotated key-fact instances and high inter-annotator agreement. With this dataset, we benchmark a wide range of automatic metrics and evaluate M2Preserve-LLM as an automated evaluator. Results show that conventional metrics are weak indicators of Completeness, whereas M2Preserve-LLM produces more structured and interpretable assessments. Further analysis reveals that simplification systems vary more in how much source content they retain than in how faithfully they render the facts they include, pointing to content selection and fact retention as central challenges in simplification.

paper.title: In Vino Veritas and Vulnerabilities: Examining LLM Safety via Drunk Language Inducement

author.affiliation: School of Computer Science and Engineering, UNSW Sydney, Australia; School of Computing and Information Systems, the University of Melbourne, Australia
School of Computer Science and Engineering, UNSW Sydney, Australia

paper.abstract: WARNING: Contains offensive/hateful speech, profanity, and other potentially triggering content. Humans are susceptible to undesirable behaviours and privacy leaks under the influence of alcohol. This paper investigates drunk language, i.e., text that mimics linguistic patterns commonly associated with alcohol intoxication, as a potential driver for safety failures in large language models (LLMs), thereby affecting the trustworthiness of NLG systems. We investigate three mechanisms for inducing drunk language in LLMs: persona-based prompting, causal fine-tuning, and reinforcement-based post-training. When evaluated on five LLMs, we observe increased susceptibility to jailbreaking on JailbreakBench (even in the presence of defences) and privacy leaks on ConfAIde compared to the base LLMs and several previously reported approaches. Using a combination of manual evaluation, LLM-based evaluators, along with analysis of error categories, our findings suggest a correspondence between linguistic patterns associated with human intoxication and LLM response induced with drunk language based on the three mechanisms. The simplicity and efficiency of our drunk language inducement highlight potential risks in current LLM safety mechanisms.

paper.title: Beyond Fine-Tuning: In-Context Learning and Chain-of-Thought for Reasoned Distractor Generation

author.affiliation: School of Computing, Macquarie University, Australia; College of Engineering and Computing in Al-Lith, Umm Al-Qura University, Saudi Arabia
School of Computing, Macquarie University, Australia
School of Computer Sciences and Information Technology, Adelaide University, Australia

paper.abstract: Distractor generation (DG) remains a labor-intensive task that still significantly depends on domain experts. The task focuses on generating plausible yet incorrect options, known as distractors, for multiple-choice questions. A reliable distractor must be contextually relevant to the question and able to mislead examinees through implicit reasoning when identifying the correct answer. While a recent method integrates fine-tuning pre-trained encoder-decoder models with contrastive learning to generate semantically relevant distractors for a given question-answer, it often fails to capture the underlying reasoning process that experts utilize when selecting distractors in benchmarks. In this paper, we explore large language models (LLMs) reasoning for DG through in-context learning with unsupervised semantic retrieval for selecting few-shot examples. We design a rationale-augmented DG framework that jointly generates distractors and their rationales for a given question-answer. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks, with varying average distractor lengths and domains, demonstrate that prompting LLMs with few-shot examples substantially improves the performance compared to recent DG models. It outperforms recent approaches and achieves state-of-the-art results in generating reasoned distractors that align with human-labeled benchmarks.

paper.title: Automating Multi-Hop RAG Evaluation via TRIAD: From Context Extraction to Validated Dataset Generation

author.affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Innsbruck, Austria
Department of Computer Science, University of Innsbruck, Austria

paper.abstract: Recent advances in LLMs and the adoption of RAG systems in industry have created a need for domain-specific question-answer datasets that can assess RAG performance on proprietary data. Existing datasets, such as HotpotQA, challenge current RAG systems on Wikipedia-based knowledge, but they cannot be transferred directly to domain-specific settings. A comprehensive evaluation of RAG system quality requires both multi-hop queries and unanswerable questions. This paper introduces TRIAD, a three-stage automated dataset generation approach. First, it generates question– answer (QA) pairs for the domain-specific knowledge base of a RAG system. Second, a validator checks each QA-pair in a feedback loop. Third, the QA pairs are extended with relevance-labeled context documents for downstream evaluation. We evaluate this approach against the established MuSiQue and HotpotQA datasets. The results show that the generated dataset exhibits similar performance trends across different RAG setups, while human validation indicates that the questions are suitable for evaluating a domain-specific RAG system. The code used to generate the dataset and all validation results are available in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/lorenzbrehme/triad).

paper.title: Can LLM Coding Agents Reason About Time Series?

author.affiliation: Charles University, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Institute of Formal and Applied Linguistics
Charles University, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Institute of Formal and Applied Linguistics
Charles University, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Institute of Formal and Applied Linguistics

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used for automated decision-making systems in finance, healthcare, or environmental monitoring. Time series data are ubiquitous in these fields, yet hard to process automatically. Can time series be analyzed by LLM agents? We examine three approaches: providing the agent with raw numerical data, using the LLM as a coding agent, or a combination of both. In the coding agent setup, the model iteratively queries the data using Python code. Using two time series understanding benchmarks, we show that agents with code access can outperform models processing raw data by up to 10%. However, even the best performing agent still answers about 22–34% of the questions incorrectly. To get insights into models’ strategies and reasoning gaps, we analyze the model outputs with a strong LLM judge. Our analysis reveals that coding agents can select appropriate statistical tests, but often miss important nuances. Meanwhile, models with access to raw data can reach the right conclusions using back-of-the-envelope calculations.

paper.title: Strategies for Span Labeling with Large Language Models

author.affiliation: Charles University, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Institute of Formal and Applied Linguistics
Charles University, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Institute of Formal and Applied Linguistics
Charles University, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Institute of Formal and Applied Linguistics

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for text analysis tasks, such as named entity recognition or error detection. Unlike encoder-based models, however, generative architectures lack an explicit mechanism to refer to specific parts of their input. This leads to a variety of ad-hoc prompting strategies for input text span labeling, often with inconsistent results. In this paper, we categorize these strategies into three families: tagging the whole input text, indexing numerical positions of spans, and matching generated span content. To address the limitations of content matching, we introduce LogitMatch, a new constrained decoding method that forces the model’s output to align with valid input spans. On four diverse tasks, we find that tagging-based methods are the most robust, but matching methods are competitive and more token-efficient. Our LogitMatch approach improves upon matching methods by retaining their performance while eliminating span matching issues.

paper.title: A Constraint-Based Formalism for Controlled Text Generation

author.affiliation: Univ. Bordeaux, CNRS, Bordeaux INP, LaBRI, UMR 5800, Talence, France

paper.abstract: Controlled text generation requires more than selecting words from an input representation: decisions made during realization may constrain later choices. We present a symbolic, constraint-based model of context-sensitive realization in Elvex, a feature-structure-based generation framework. Inherited feature structures encode realization requirements, while synthesized structures record realization results that can be stored in an explicit generation context and reused by other constituents. A chart-based generation algorithm schedules constituents according to information availability rather than surface order and constructs unordered or partially ordered shared forests subject to explicit linearity constraints. We evaluate synthesized-context reuse on 12 curated predicative-noun support-verb relations covering nine distinct support verbs. Full and Pre-specified each license only the 12 compatible realizations, whereas No-Context licenses 96 additional incompatible noun–support combinations. This ablation directly tests whether a lexical constraint produced during realization can restrict a later choice without being pre-specified in the input. Complementary experiments on E2E/GEM and WebNLG assess closed-domain coverage, input preservation, and local RDF realization.

paper.title: Can we use LLMs to generate data-driven patient narratives? A multi-method exploration in the oncology domain

author.affiliation: Tilburg University, Tilburg, Netherlands
Tilburg University, Tilburg, Netherlands
Netherlands Cancer Institute, Amsterdam, Netherlands
Netherlands Cancer Institute, Amsterdam, Netherlands
Tilburg University, Tilburg, Netherlands
Tilburg University, Tilburg, Netherlands

paper.abstract: Translating patient data about health-related quality of life (e.g., fatigue) to narrative feedback has the potential to enhance the interpretability and emotional resonance of key outcomes in oncology care. However, producing personalized narratives at scale is challenging. Based on advances in large language models (LLMs), this study explores whether LLMs have the potential to generate narratives that are of sufficiently high accuracy and quality to support patients’ health-related quality of life. Therefore, we generated 5500 narratives from 110 oncology patient profiles using 10 LLMs varying in size, domain specificity, and reasoning capabilities as well as 5 prompt paraphrases. Using a human validated LLM-as-judge approach, we find that LLMs generate narratives of varying accuracy, with the best model achieving over 80% in accuracy. Human evaluations show that most narratives are seen as accurately following the prompt and as coherent, but vary more for empathy and engagement. Accuracy is overall not associated with empathy or coherence and even weakly negatively associated with engagement, highlighting the importance of multi-criteria evaluation. Further research should explore how narratives can be generated in a robust way in a clinical setting and how clinicians can be meaningfully involved.

paper.title: Chain-of-Thought Depth Modulates Performance by Task and Model: Evidence from Ablation Studies Across Five Model Families

author.affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, PES University, Bangalore, India

paper.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting is widely assumed to improve language model outputs, yet recent work shows it can degrade accuracy on tasks requiring implicit pattern recognition. Prior studies treat CoT as a binary intervention and do not control for confounds such as generation-budget truncation and prompt-wording effects. We introduce a three-condition depth manipulation (no-CoT, short CoT, long CoT) and evaluate five configurations of four model families across artificial grammar learning (AGL) and natural language inference (NLI), totaling 68,872 evaluations. We report findings spanning three categories. Core: (1) three architectures produce three qualitatively different depth-accuracy patterns on grammar; (2) a task×depth crossover emerges within individual models; (3) we decompose CoT failure into mechanistically distinct response-generation and reasoning failure. Confound isolation: (4) the apparent collapse is a generation-budget artifact; (5) response failure is prompt-specific; (6) NLI findings replicate on held-out stimuli. Novel analyses: (7) item difficulty moderates CoT degradation, with easy grammars suffering the largest drop (−15.8 pp) while hard grammars lose only −3.7 pp; (8) cross-model error agreement drops substantially under deep CoT, with pairwise agreement falling from 72.7% to 42.3%; (9) cross-temperature response stability collapses under long CoT, with only 2.8% of items producing consistent outcomes across three temperatures versus 79.4% under short CoT. These results reveal that CoT effects on implicit-pattern tasks are shaped by the interaction of task structure, model architecture, prompt wording, and generation budget.

paper.title: ADR-Control: Do LLM Coding Agents Follow Architectural Decisions? An Evaluation of ADR-Grounded Code Generation

author.affiliation: FPT University, Hanoi, Vietnam
FPT University, Hanoi, Vietnam

paper.abstract: Large language models can generate code at repository scale, but they frequently violate architectural intent even when relevant design decisions are available as context. This gap mirrors a broader faithfulness problem in natural language generation: models retrieve correct evidence yet fail to apply it faithfully in their outputs. We propose ADR-Control, a framework that elevates Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) from passive documentation to active control artifacts through retrieval, constraint normalization, verification, and typed trace emission. We evaluate one bounded component of this framework: canonical ADR-constraint violation identification on fixed candidate patches under four reviewer-context conditions across five tasks from one .NET repository. Across two canonical repetitions, Structured-ADR context achieves mean canonical identification F1 of 0.746 ± 0.145, compared with 0.675 ± 0.194 for ADR-prose context. This result provides pilot evidence for bounded ADR-grounded constraint identification; it does not establish end-to-end generation superiority, verifier-gated repair success, executable correctness, or generalization beyond the pilot.

paper.title: Not All Linguistic Capabilities Degrade Equally Under Quantization

author.affiliation: Independent Researcher

paper.abstract: Low-precision quantization enables efficient LLM deployment, but its effect on distinct linguistic capabilities is poorly characterised: prior evaluations report aggregate metrics (perplexity, task accuracy), obscuring differential degradation. We evaluate four instruction-tuned models (Qwen 2.5-7B, Mistral 7B, Llama 3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B) across four NLG tasks (summarisation, dialogue, data-to-text, simplification) and five quantization conditions (4-bit AWQ/GPTQ/GGUF, 2-bit GGUF, 16-bit baseline), measuring lexical accuracy (ROUGE), syntactic well-formedness (grammar error rate), factual consistency (AlignScore), and discourse/instruction-following (GPT-4o-mini judge). Across 92 conditions (≈500 samples each): (1) Friedman tests reject uniform degradation in 84% of model-task-bit-width combinations (p < 0.05); (2) factual consistency is more stable than grammar at 4-bit across all architectures (AlignScore mean change: −1.8%, d = −0.355; grammar degrades more in 18/27 cells, Bonferroni-corrected); (3) grammar direction is architecture-dependent: Qwen degrades (+19.0%) while Llama improves (−12.8%); (4) grammar improvement on dialogue (3/4 models) is not a length artefact: per-sample length–grammar correlations are near zero, and Mistral falsifies the length hypothesis (output +34.4% longer, grammar rate −37.9%). Compression does not yield a single robustness profile; it induces capability-specific changes depending on architecture, task, and quantization method.

paper.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Must Move Beyond Factual Grounding to Represent Diverse Opinions

author.affiliation: Amazon.com

paper.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are built on an unexamined assumption: that queries have correct answers and retrieval should converge toward them. This position paper argues that this creates a factual bias where RAG systems optimize for reducing epistemic uncertainty while ignoring the aleatoric uncertainty, inherent in opinion-rich content. The consequences go beyond technical limitations: due to risk of minority voice erasure and risk of opinion manipulation. To address this, we formalize opinion-aware retrieval through uncertainty quantification and derive a unified objective using the Wasserstein distance. As an existence proof, we present Opinion-Aware RAG (O-RAG), which enriches documents with LLM-extracted, entity-linked opinion metadata before indexing. Across e-commerce seller forums and public hotel reviews, O-RAG reduces Wasserstein distance to corpus-level sentiment distributions by 18–48%, and human evaluators preferred its responses 79.2% of the time. We close with a research agenda for opinion-aware RAG.

paper.title: ViInfoSum: A Novel Dataset for Multimodal Summarization in Vietnamese

paper.abstract: Multimodal Summarization requires the exploration of mutual information from multimodal data such as text and graphics. Although this task has been well-studied on high resource languages such as English, the development in methodology of this task on low-resource languages such as Vietnamese is limited. In this study, we introduce ViInfoSum, a novel dataset for evaluating Multimodal Summarization methods in Vietnamese. Evaluation of baselines for abstractive text summarization and OCR-based image captioning methods show that they are not effective in determining correct entities from multimodal inputs, which results in wrong summarization. To this end, we propose ViInfoSummer, a novel method that learn to indicate entities correctly from multimodal inputs which leads to performance improvement on the ViInfoSum dataset for Multimodal Summarization in Vietnamese.

paper.title: From Tables to Quantified Statements: Evaluating LLM Inference Generation through Executable Verification

author.affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana Champaign

paper.abstract: LLMs can generate fluent descriptions from tables, but their outputs may remain logically unsupported by the structured data. We introduce STAT-TO-TEXT1, a controlled task in which LLMs generate quantified natural language inferences from statistical tables using quantified constructions such as all, some, no, and most. To evaluate these inferences, we use an LLM generated Python checker code which when executed verifies the corresponding truth conditions against the table. We compare four open-weight LLMs across model families and scales, evaluating faithfulness, logical accuracy, table coverage, and diversity. Our results show that model scale and family matter, with the largest model (GPT-OSS-120B) consistently producing the most faithful inferences without sacrificing greater table coverage and quantifier diversity, as opposed to smaller models. These findings are supported by human annotation, which shows that the automated checker closely aligns with human judgments.

paper.title: Metric Cards Make Blind Spots Legible

author.affiliation: Technische Universität Berlin
CLCG, University of Groningen; German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI)

paper.abstract: Model-based evaluation metrics for large language models (LLMs) are known to be brittle to slight input perturbations: prior work uncovers many such blind spots, but reports them as isolated findings, leaving practitioners without a coherent picture of any one metric’s measurement profile. We propose metric cards – short, structured reports that aggregate perturbation-test results into an interpretable analysis of a metric’s strengths and failure modes – and a pipeline that drafts them automatically. Reproducing established perturbation-test setups on machine translation, summarization, and open-ended generation, we (i) prompt three LLMs to draft metric cards from the test results and validate their alignment against human-written references, and (ii) run an exploratory authoring study (n = 4 authors, 8 cards, plus two external raters, and three frontier LLM judges) on whether LLM drafts help authors write better cards. LLM drafts align closely with human cards on retrieval and conclusion dimensions but still produce factual errors, so they are best used as scaffolds in a human-in-the-loop pipeline. The drafts function as cognitive scaffolds, not shortcuts. They do not reduce wall-clock writing time, yet authors rate them as helpful structural prototypes, and external raters’ scores do not distinguish assisted from unassisted cards. The three independent LLM judges agree closely with one another but barely correlate with humans, adding to the evidence that off-the-shelf judges require validation before substituting for human evaluation of metric cards.

paper.title: Augmenting Lecture Information via Redundancy-Filtered LLM Slide Descriptions for Blind and Low-Vision Students

author.affiliation: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology; University of Applied Sciences Karlsruhe
Karlsruhe Institute of Technology

paper.abstract: Slides in video lectures often contain information that is inaccessible to blind and low-vision students unless explicitly described. Although previous studies have addressed this accessibility gap, existing solutions often fail to align visual content with spoken narration, leading to redundant or omitted details. This paper presents an automated method for generating slide descriptions to enhance lecture content. A large language model refines them to eliminate redundancy with respect to spoken narration. Experimental results demonstrate that the system can effectively filter the information already mentioned by the lecturer, reaching word count compressions of up to 65%, while preserving important information. Our findings suggest that careful prompt design can directly balance efficiency with content preservation.

paper.title: PromptDistill: Query-based Selective Token Retention in Intermediate Layers for Efficient Large Language Model Inference

author.affiliation: Singapore University of Technology and Design, Singapore

paper.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) tackle increasingly complex tasks and longer documents, their inference cost becomes a major bottleneck. To address this, we propose PromptDistill, a novel, training-free method that improves inference efficiency while preserving generation quality. PromptDistill identifies and retains the most informative tokens by leveraging early-layer attention, preserving their hidden states while reducing computation in later layers. Unlike previous methods such as H2O, SnapKV, and GemFilter, which perform compression only after full input processing, or ignore contextual dependencies, PromptDistill dynamically allocates computation to relevant tokens while maintaining global context. Experiments on LLaMA 3.1 8B, Phi 3.5 Mini, Qwen2 7B/14B, Phi 3 128k across LongBench, InfBench, and Needle in a Haystack demonstrate that PromptDistill achieves substantial efficiency gains with minimal quality loss. With a single-stage selection strategy, it outperforms GemFilter, H2O, and SnapKV, achieving an overall 1% to 5% performance improvement with faster inference. Additionally, we explore multi-stage selection, which further improves efficiency while maintaining strong generation performance. These results demonstrate the adaptability of LLM hidden representations and provide valuable insights into optimizing inference for long-context scenarios. We have made our implementations publicly available.

paper.title: FJ-Guard: Persistence-Guided Training-Free Defense for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems

author.affiliation: KDDI Research Inc., Fujimino, Japan

paper.abstract: Multi-Agent Systems (MASs) built from large language model (LLM) agents can improve reasoning through inter-agent collaboration. However, the inter-agent influence that enables collaboration also allows an adversarial claim from a few agents to spread to honest agents and corrupt the collective answer. To defend against such attacks, prior MAS defenses often rely on learned detectors that require interaction data and training before deployment. To address these limitations, we propose FJ-Guard, a training-free framework that detects adversarial agents at runtime and remediates their propagated influence. Our key idea is that, for an attack to propagate, the adversarial agent tends to persist with the target answer and its supporting reasoning, while honest agents are influenced by their peers and shift their reasoning. We capture this behavior by measuring how persistently each agent’s reasoning in later rounds remains tied to its initial reasoning rather than shifting toward its neighbors, using lexical similarity as a training-free signal. Our evaluation across diverse settings, including prompt injection, memory attacks, tool attacks, and varying adversary ratios, shows that FJ-Guard identifies adversarial agents without training and improves the final collective answer through runtime remediation. On GPT-4o-mini, it reduces the average attack success rate to less than half that of an existing self-supervised defense that requires training, while improving answer accuracy.

paper.title: CAAF: Confidence and Agreement-Aware Fusion for Multi-LLM Ensembles

author.affiliation: TCS Research, India
TCS Research, India

paper.abstract: Integrating multiple Large Language Models (LLMs) into ensembles improves robustness and generalization, yet existing methods often rely on coarse selection or static weighting, failing to integrate trustworthy information at a granular level. We introduce CAAF (Confidence and Agreement-Aware Fusion), a transformer-based encoder-decoder framework designed for dynamic, token-level fusion of diverse LLM outputs. CAAF utilizes a dual-source reliability signal combining LLM self-reported confidence with cross-model semantic agreement to guide the generation process. These signals are injected statically into encoder embeddings and dynamically as attention biases in the decoder, enabling the model to prioritize reliable content from heterogeneous sources. We evaluate CAAF on a comprehensive suite of twelve knowledge-intensive datasets, featuring an ensemble of heterogeneous LLMs. Across twelve knowledge-intensive datasets and averaged over four metrics (Rouge-L, Rouge-LSum, Meteor, and BERTScore-F1), CAAF attains mean scores of 48.03 and 48.11 using models with only 160M and 330M parameters. In comparison, LLM-Blender achieves average scores of 44.01 (700M) and 45.14 (3B), while GPT-4 based fusion yields mean scores of 44.92.

paper.title: Towards Green Text Generation: Memory-Based Speculative Decoding

author.affiliation: Utrecht University

paper.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates text generation with large language models by letting a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large verifier checks in a single forward pass. We introduce Olifant, a draft model built on a memory-based classifier. It predicts the next token from a four-token window in under 0.3 ms on CPU, requiring no GPU, no backpropagation, and no accelerator memory. We measure throughput and energy under two verifier regimes on consumer hardware. Without a KV cache, drafting is nearly free: a domain-matched Olifant model reaches 38.1% acceptance on EU legal text, delivering 2.43× throughput and 2.51× lower energy per token than the neural verifier model alone. With a KV-cached verifier, itself a ∼10× energy saver, drafting costs matter: a TinyLlama draft model halves throughput and triples energy despite high acceptance, whereas Olifant still yields 1.25× throughput and the lowest energy in the study (93 J per 100 tokens, 14× below the uncached baseline). We further show that KV caching decouples time from energy: verification of longer drafts raises power draw, shifting the energy-optimal draft length below the speed-optimal one. Speculative decoding is not dead in the age of fast verifiers, provided drafting is nearly free.

paper.title: Decomposed Entailment for Factuality Checking and Hallucination Detection

author.affiliation: Université Paris-Saclay, Gif-sur-Yvette, France
Université Paris-Saclay, CEA, List, Palaiseau, France
Université Paris-Saclay, CEA, List, Palaiseau, France

paper.abstract: The reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs) is often compromised by factual inconsistencies, including hallucinations—cases where generated content is not supported by the underlying source. We present HallDetect, a lightweight, reference-free, and black-box framework for hallucination detection that we evaluate not only on summarization but across a broader range of source-grounded generation settings. HallDetect builds on decomposition-based factuality evaluation: generated content is decomposed into atomic claims, each verified by a compact encoder-based entailment model through a contrastive formulation over a multi-scale library of source chunks, and aggregated with an asymmetric score in which a single confidently contradicted claim flags the response. Under a controlled protocol in which all methods share the same 4-bit quantized backbones and consumer-grade hardware budget, HallDetect outperforms comparably resourced generative and embedding-based baselines on three of four benchmarks while remaining stable across backbone families, and yields a claim-to-span audit trail that localizes each error.

paper.title: What Did My Adapter Break? A Generation-Level Evaluation of Adaptation and Retention in PEFT-Adapted LLMs

author.affiliation: Efi Arazi School of Computer Science, Reichman University, Israel; Data Science Institute, Reichman University, Israel
Efi Arazi School of Computer Science, Reichman University, Israel
Data Science Institute, Reichman University, Israel

paper.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning enables instruction-tuned large language models to adapt to new tasks and domains, but it can also destabilize outputs the base model previously generated reliably. Existing analyses commonly measure such degradation through aggregate benchmark deltas, which reveal overall performance changes but not which outputs fail or how severely. We introduce a dual-axis, generation-level evaluation framework that measures adaptation and retention through repeated generations. Our Negative Shift measure identifies prompts whose correct-generation rate collapses after adaptation. Using this framework, we compare LoRA, DoRA, VeRA, and our proposed UIOrthoLoRA across learning-rate and capacity sweeps on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Gemma-3-12B-IT. The retention–adaptation trade-off is highly sensitive to learning rate: LoRA and DoRA exhibit abrupt degradation under aggressive optimization, whereas structurally constrained parameterizations degrade more gradually. At comparable target performance, moving from small to medium adapter capacity often improves retention, although gains are not monotonic. UIOrthoLoRA, a spectrum-aware adapter that restricts directional adaptation to the low-energy spectral tail, improves the observed trade-off relative to the evaluated baselines under constrained parameter budgets.

paper.title: Translating Classical Poetry into Modern Prose

author.affiliation: Computational Linguistics, University of Potsdam, Germany
National Research Council, Ottawa, Canada

paper.abstract: We built a dataset for the task of poem-to-prose translation from 13th-17th Century Telugu classical poetry to contemporary Telugu and English prose, which we call (Padyam2Gadyam). The dataset consists of 600 poems and their human-verified Telugu and English prose translations. We evaluated 2 machine translation systems and 5 contemporary Large Language Models (LLMs) on their ability to do zero-shot poem-to-prose translation into Telugu and English using this dataset. Our results indicate that while the general purpose LLMs are better than the machine translation systems, there are systematic issues with the generation and evaluation of prose translation in both languages across systems.

paper.title: Self-Verification is All You Need To Pass The Japanese Bar Examination

author.affiliation: Keio University

paper.abstract: Despite rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), achieving reliable performance on highly professional and structured examinations remains a significant challenge. The Japanese bar examination is a particularly demanding benchmark, requiring not only advanced legal reasoning but also strict adherence to complex answer formats that involve joint evaluation of multiple propositions. While recent studies have reported improvements by decomposing such questions into simpler true– false judgments, these approaches have not been systematically evaluated under the original exam format and scoring scheme, leaving open the question of whether they truly capture exam-level competence. In this paper, we present a self-verification model trained on a newly constructed dataset that faithfully replicates the authentic format and evaluation scale of the exam. Our model is able to exceed the official passing score when evaluated on the actual exam scale, marking the first demonstration, to our knowledge, of an LLM passing the Japanese bar examination without altering its original question structure or scoring rules. We further conduct extensive comparisons with alternative strategies, including multi-agent inference and decomposition-based supervision, and find that these methods fail to achieve comparable performance. Our results highlight the importance of format-faithful supervision and consistency verification, and suggest that carefully designed single-model approaches can outperform more complex systems in high-stakes professional reasoning tasks. Our dataset and codes are publicly available.

paper.title: Automatic vs. Human Evaluation: Benchmarking 26 Automatic Metrics for Clinical Discharge Summaries

author.affiliation: Julius Center for Health Sciences and Primary Care, University Medical Center Utrecht, Utrecht University
Julius Center for Health Sciences and Primary Care, University Medical Center Utrecht, Utrecht University
Team AI, Operations department, University Medical Center Utrecht
Team AI, Operations department, University Medical Center Utrecht
Julius Center for Health Sciences and Primary Care, University Medical Center Utrecht, Utrecht University
Julius Center for Health Sciences and Primary Care, University Medical Center Utrecht, Utrecht University

paper.abstract: Automatic evaluation metrics are widely used to assess the quality of clinical summaries. However, most existing automatic metrics were not designed to capture clinically critical errors and were primarily developed and validated on English data, raising concerns about their applicability in non-English clinical settings. In this work, we examine how well commonly used automatic metrics reflect clinically critical criteria in Dutch. We benchmark 26 evaluation metrics on real-world LLM-generated clinical discharge summaries and correlate their scores with clinically critical errors, including hallucinations, omissions, and trivial facts. Our results show that standard automatic metrics do not capture hallucination errors in this setting. Specific lightweight source-based metrics may provide useful signals for identifying omission-related errors and trivial facts, highlighting their potential for prioritizing human review efforts in real-world settings.

paper.title: Hierarchical Experience Memory for Multi-Agent Task Planning and Subtask Guidance

author.affiliation: Independent

paper.abstract: This study presents Hierarchical Memory Planning, a self-evolving hierarchical memory framework designed to improve multi-agent task planning for complex reasoning tasks. The framework enhances the planning capability of large language model (LLM) agents by accumulating experience from previous task trajectories and grounding future decomposition decisions in retrieved memory. In Hierarchical Memory Planning, a centralized meta-agent decomposes each user query into subtasks and assigns them to specialized subagents, while a plan-level memory retrieves similar historical cases and distills reusable insights from comparisons between lower-scoring and higher-scoring trajectories. To reduce the mismatch between high-level planning and subagent execution, we further introduce a subagent-level memory mechanism for task planning, which augments each raw subtask produced by the initial plan with task-execution guidance distilled from prior subagent experience. This hierarchical design assigns distinct functions to the two memory levels: plan-level memory guides global decomposition, while subagent-level memory improves the executability of individual subtasks. Through experiments on DROP-eval and IIRC-eval, using 150 training examples from IIRC and DROP as the experience pool, Hierarchical Memory Planning achieves accuracies of 37.0 and 43.5, respectively. These results indicate that hierarchical experience memory can support multi-agent task planning under the studied setting.

paper.title: Dynamic Intent-Driven API Pruning for Tool Learning in Small Language Models

author.affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, National Chung Hsing University, Taiwan
Department of Computer Science and Engineering, National Chung Hsing University, Taiwan
Department of Computer Science and Engineering, National Chung Hsing University, Taiwan
Smart Sustainable New Agriculture Research Center (SMARTer), National Chung Hsing University, Taiwan
Department of Computer Science and Engineering, National Chung Hsing University, Taiwan

paper.abstract: Small Language Models (SLMs) struggle with tool calling, in part because a single API document often serves several usage intents and bundles the parameters of all of them into one schema, even though only a few are relevant to any given query. Providing the complete document forces the model to infer the intended usage scenario and its parameters at the same time, which lengthens the prompt and creates parameter ambiguity within a single API. We propose Dynamic Intent-Driven API Pruning. In an offline stage, an LLM decomposes each API document into Intent Units, each pairing an Intent Scenario with a Key Parameter Subset. At inference time, two-stage intent retrieval identifies the intents that match the query, and Dynamic Flat Union merges their parameter subsets into a query-specific pruned schema, keeping several intents rather than committing to a possibly incorrect top-1 choice. On 35 real-world APIs from ToolBench, our method improves argument correctness over Simulated Trial-and-Error while producing shorter prompts, with the gains concentrated on APIs that support multiple usage intents. Ablation studies confirm that both intent-driven pruning and Dynamic Flat Union reduce intra-API parameter ambiguity.

paper.title: Confident by Default: A Longitudinal Study of Style Drift and Convergence Across Large Language Model Providers

author.affiliation: Department of Information and Communications Engineering, Aalto University, Espoo, Finland
Department of Information and Communications Engineering, Aalto University, Espoo, Finland

paper.abstract: Large language models handle millions of daily interactions, and their default style shapes user trust and reliance. Yet evaluations rarely track provider defaults across releases. In this work, we measure style drift in five model families across five generations from 2024 to mid 2026. The analysis contains 6780 assistant turns from 40 sensitive questions and five everyday conversational scenarios, collected without a custom system prompt and scored with lexical and style metrics. Across releases, conversational responses become more linguistically certain and use less supportive language, hedging, positive emotion, and professional-referral language. Negative emotion also rises. The increase in certainty is large (Hedges’ g = 1.28), and the share of conversations containing a professional-referral phrase falls from 51% to 2%. Certainty and professional-referral language shift consistently across all five families and scenarios, and providers converge on both dimensions. Sensitive answers also become more certain and less supportive. Convergent style shifts can affect reliance, emotional support, and help-seeking behavior of users. This work highlights that default style is an important user-impact dimension for longitudinal model evaluation.

paper.title: Generating Critical Questions for Arguments: A Large-Scale Analysis of Prompting and Reranking Strategies

author.affiliation: Bauhaus-Universität Weimar
Bauhaus-Universität Weimar

paper.abstract: Critical Question Generation aims to create questions that challenge an argument’s assumptions, evidence, or reasoning. But what exactly does “challenge” mean? This paper first discusses the origins of the idea of critical questions and proposes a definition that accounts for the audience dependence of arguments. Its main contribution is a large-scale empirical study on the CQs-Gen benchmark, covering 42 language models, 18 prompting strategies, supervised fine-tuning, and a generate-then-select approach. We find that our proposed architecture with a fine-tuned ModernBERT reranker achieves 82.4% on the CQs-Gen evaluation score, surpassing the winner of the ArgMining 2025 shared task by 14.8 percentage points. We test the prevailing assumption that criticality can be derived from argumentation scheme templates and show this assumption to be incomplete: scheme-aware prompting can even degrade performance (by around 4% in 23 of 34 open-weight models, with a directionally consistent but weaker effect in proprietary systems). We also observe that compact fine-tuned models surpass larger zero-shot systems. Together, these results suggest that generating practically useful critical questions benefits from context-sensitive generation and selection rather than scheme-template matching.

paper.title: From Sounds to Symbols: A Survey of Phonetically and Phonologically Informed Language Generation

author.affiliation: Department of Computer Science, The University of Sheffield, UK; Department of Computer Science, The University of Manchester, UK
Department of Computer Science, The University of Sheffield, UK
Department of Computer Science, The University of Manchester, UK

paper.abstract: Text, although written using symbols and characters, is not void of connection to the predominantly spoken form of language. Whilst syntax and semantics are the cornerstones of meaningful text, a substantial portion of human communication relies heavily on the specific sounds and sound patterns observed in language. In this survey paper, we present an outline of the areas of computational linguistics, specifically natural language generation (NLG), that are either dependent upon, or benefit from, an additional understanding of phonetics and phonology. We cover a range of subdisciplines, from practical areas such as and grapheme-to-phoneme conversion (G2P) to creative endeavours such as poetry and humour generation. We aim for this overview to situate the role of phonetics and phonology in NLG, and invite the community at-large to consider how the study of such features may be able to positively impact different domains through fusing characteristics of both speech and text.

paper.title: Do as I Say, Not as You Do: Assessing Public Versus Practitioner Perspectives on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Language Technologies

author.affiliation: Department of Computer Science, The University of Sheffield, UK; Department of Computer Science, The University of Manchester, UK
Department of Computer Science, The University of Manchester, UK

paper.abstract: With the public awareness of artificial intelligence (AI) applications such as large language models (LLMs) and generative text-to-video models reaching unprecedented levels, there is an increasing need to reconcile the perspectives held by informed practitioners, who research and develop these technologies, with the interests and opinions of the general public, who constitute the majority of people impacted by technological developments. In this work, we survey practitioners (i.e., academics and industry professionals) alongside members of the general public on perspectives relating to pertinent areas of artificial intelligence, including perceived benefit and risk, the ability for models to achieve consciousness and output art, and the use of copyright protected material for model training. Alongside comparisons of diverse perspectives on these topics, we additionally contextualise the findings with a discussion of relevant literature that supports and refutes the myriad observed stances.

paper.title: Structured Critique Generation Mitigates Toxification in Self-Critique Alignment

author.affiliation: University of Tsukuba
National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology
University of Tsukuba

paper.abstract: Self-critique alignment, in which a model iteratively evaluates and revises its own outputs according to a predefined set of principles, provides a scalable alternative to human-labeled preference data. However, the critique step, typically performed in free-text form, introduces ambiguity that degrades training data quality. We identify a novel phenomenon we term toxification: a failure mode in the Supervised Learning Constitutional AI (SL-CAI) pipeline where a safe response becomes harmful after revision, driven by vague or context-insensitive free-text critiques. To suppress toxification, we propose Structured Critique Generation (SCG), which replaces free-text critique with a structured output format containing an explicit violation flag and a reason field. When no violation is detected, revision is skipped entirely, limiting toxification across revision steps; otherwise, the structured reason guides revision directly. We evaluate SCG by fine-tuning Llama 3.1 8B Instruct on data generated under six conditions varying principle-ordering strategies and critique formats. SCG substantially improves the refusal rate on unsafe prompts compared to the conventional SL-CAI.

paper.title: EuroAlpaca: Task-Preserving Localisation of Instruction Data for European Languages

author.affiliation: Scientific Research, Telefónica Innovación Digital, Barcelona, Spain; Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, Barcelona, Spain
Scientific Research, Telefónica Innovación Digital, Barcelona, Spain
Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, Barcelona, Spain

paper.abstract: Machine translation (MT) offers a scalable way to extend English instruction-tuning data to multiple languages, but it can distort task-critical constraints and required outputs, creating corrupted training examples and degrading models trained on such data. We introduce EuroAlpaca, a task-preserving localisation pipeline and near-parallel resource covering 50 European languages and regional varieties, together with European-IFEval, a multilingual benchmark for verifiable instruction following. Depending on the example, our pipeline applies field-wise MT while preserving task-critical content or reconstructs a task-equivalent target-language instance, followed by validation of cross-field coherence and target-language consistency. Across LoRA experiments with four LLMs, training on directly translated data improves ROUGE-L and FBERT on the Aya Evaluation Suite, but reduces accuracy on European-IFEval by 29.8% relative to the unadapted baseline. In contrast, adaptation with EuroAlpaca improves accuracy by 12.9% over the same baseline, reversing the degradation caused by direct MT, while also achieving the highest ROUGE-L and FBERT scores on Aya. These results show that preserving task semantics is essential for multilingual instruction tuning.

paper.title: Mid-Utterance Transition Control for Audio Commentary Generation

author.affiliation: The University of Tokyo; National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology
National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology
National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Audio commentary generation enhances spectator engagement by describing ongoing events. A critical challenge in this domain is promptly reacting to newly emerging events while maintaining coherent transitions. Existing approaches face a fundamental trade-off: waiting for utterance completion causes delays, whereas immediate transitions risk unnatural mid-word truncation. Despite its importance, mid-utterance transition control remains underexplored. We formulate this problem as deciding when to terminate an ongoing utterance and how to connect it to the next. We compare four human-inspired strategies: immediate interruption, chunk-based interruption at syntactic boundaries, LLM-inserted break points, and LLM-generated shortened closures. Our experiments on a fast-paced game quantify the trade-off between responsiveness and naturalness. Human evaluation reveals that natural transitions do not always require complete sentences; interrupting at clear linguistic boundaries preserves responsiveness while avoiding unnatural truncation.

paper.title: Effort and Confidence: Surface Markers in Reasoning Traces Predict Correctness on Insight Puzzles

author.affiliation: City St George’s, University of London
City St George’s, University of London; The Alan Turing Institute

paper.abstract: Multimodal large language models with reasoning abilities produce extended thinking traces before committing to an answer. Whether these natural language self-descriptions of the models’ problem-solving behaviours faithfully reflect their internal uncertainty, and whether that uncertainty affects the committed output, are open questions with significant implications for how we evaluate and trust model reasoning processes. We present a focused study that investigates this relationship using insight puzzles, which require a non-linear reinterpretation of semantic, phonetic or visual clues and thereby produce a discrete resolution event with a characteristic surface signature. Our study reveals three findings. First, the correctness signal in reasoning traces across four insight domains is largely recoverable from surface effort markers, where a simple six-feature keyword-based classifier matches or outperforms the richer semantic models we tested, predicting correctness at average precision 0.85 against a 0.62 base rate and rising to 0.89 once an additional trace-derived confidence feature is added. Second, this signal is only partly shared with mathematical reasoning. Length and duration effort markers predict correctness on math traces too, but the hedging and resolution language that distinguishes insight traces is largely absent from math, where models express difficulty through trace length rather than uncertainty and confidence markers. Third, the model’s self-reported confidence is systematically miscalibrated relative to the signal present in its own trace, with an external classifier reading the same text roughly five times better calibrated.

paper.title: Reasoning–Answer Entailment Under GRPO and DPO Fine-Tuning

author.affiliation: Department of Methodology, Statistics & Data Science, Utrecht University, Utrecht, The Netherlands
Department of Methodology, Statistics & Data Science, Utrecht University, Utrecht, The Netherlands

paper.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting can improve the problem-solving ability of large language models (LLMs), but a generated rationale does not always reflect the process by which a model reaches its answer, which limits the value of CoT for oversight and safety monitoring. We compare two post-training methods, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), on one measurable component of this problem: reasoning–answer entailment, whether the reasoning a model states supports the answer it gives. Entailment is a necessary condition for faithful reasoning, not a certificate of it, and we scope our claims accordingly. Across four scales of the Qwen2.5-Instruct family (1.5B– 14B) on GSM8K, we evaluate eight fine-tuned models on accuracy, reliability, and entailment metrics computed from persisted per-example generations, report bootstrap confidence intervals and paired significance tests, and assess the robustness of LLM-as-a-judge scoring with two independent judges. GRPO yields significantly higher entailment at every scale (margins of +.14 to +.31, all p < 10−7) and sweeps all metrics at 7B, while DPO matches GRPO’s greedy and pass@1 accuracy at 14B at lower training cost (self-consistency still favors GRPO). The methods fail differently. GRPO produces internally consistent rationales even when its answers are wrong; DPO’s stated reasoning fails to entail a majority of its correct answers at every scale, consistent with the DPO recipe optimizing answer style rather than the reasoning–answer link. A forensic analysis attributes the mid-scale (3B) collapse of both methods largely to output-format failure rather than lost reasoning ability, and a headline 14B judge-score gap does not survive re-evaluation with a second judge.

paper.title: Trust Stack for Mental Health AI: A Survey of Calibration across Human, Interaction, and AI Layers

author.affiliation: National Institute of Informatics (NII), Japan; University of Amsterdam, the Netherlands
Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, the Netherlands

Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, the Netherlands

Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, the Netherlands

paper.abstract: Language-based AI is increasingly deployed for mental health support, yet trust is evaluated in interdisciplinary but operationally misaligned ways: NLP and AI work measures robustness, safety, privacy, and explanations, while psychotherapy, HCI, and regulatory work emphasize therapeutic fidelity, lived experience, empathy, and reliance. Empathetic chatbots can elicit strong user trust without commensurate safety, while safer systems are under-trusted when their boundaries are opaque, a calibration gap no single community owns. Through a structured scoping synthesis of 61 papers, we survey this landscape into a three-layer framework separating (L1) human-oriented trust, (L2) interaction-oriented trustworthiness, and (L3) AI-oriented trustworthiness, and map five stakeholder perspectives onto these layers. We outline a research agenda for building socio-technically aligned trustworthy AI for mental health support, highlighting that the central objective should shift from maximizing perceived trust to calibrating human trust to demonstrated interaction- and AI-level trustworthiness.

paper.title: Large Language Models for Data Augmentation in Product Matching

author.affiliation: Charles University, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Prague, Czech Republic
Charles University, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Prague, Czech Republic

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for natural language processing tasks in data-scarce domains. In this paper, we study their application to product matching, the task of deciding whether two product descriptions from two different e-shops describe the same product. We use three recent LLMs (Llama 3.2, Gemma 3, and DeepSeek-R1) to enrich product records in product-matching datasets with descriptions generated from the limited available information, and we show that the generated descriptions improve the performance of both LLM-based and traditional machine-learning matchers.

paper.title: Persona as a Dynamical System: Attractor-Based Character Control for Neural Text Generation

author.affiliation: Department of Computer Science, National Tsing Hua University, Taiwan
Department of Computer Science, National Tsing Hua University, Taiwan
Department of Computer Science, National Tsing Hua University, Taiwan

paper.abstract: Prompting and activation steering are the two common ways of holding a language model in a persona, and both are static: the prompt is a fixed instruction, the steering vector a fixed offset, and when a long adversarial dialogue pushes the model out of character, nothing in either mechanism pushes back. We treat persona maintenance as a control problem instead. The Cognitive Attractor Layer (CAL) is a training-free module attached to one decoder block at inference time. It keeps a 14-dimensional latent state whose coordinates are named psychological axes (emotion, belief, goal fields), updates it each token by a contractive linear recurrence with a restoring force toward a persona centre, writes the result back into the residual stream, and biases decoding by the remaining distance to the centre. We give conditions under which this is provably an attractor, and, since a system built to return could be accused of returning trivially, separate the two sources of contraction and show the restoring force does work that inertia alone cannot. In a shock-recovery protocol the contrast between CAL and a matched static-steering control reproduces on two model families (Qwen3-8B and Mistral-7B), and a 30-annotator human study confirms the advantage is visible to readers; personas are doubly dissociable in the latent state and in generated text; and activation patching with sparse autoencoders places the effect in a persona-specific layer band. A single-field belief transplant is clearly present in the latent but cannot override a strong prompt-level persona in the text, a boundary we report as a finding.

paper.title: Content Determination Is the Faithfulness Bottleneck: A Computable-Oracle Benchmark for Faithful LLM Explanations of Guardrail Decisions

author.affiliation: University College of Engineering, BIT Campus, Anna University

paper.abstract: When an AI agent’s tool call is allowed or blocked by a policy gateway, an LLM typically generates the natural-language explanation shown to users and auditors. We study this as a data-to-text generation task with an unusual property. The input includes an executable decision function, so the correct content of the explanation (the minimal sufficient reason for the decision) is exactly computable. This yields a reference-free, fully automatic evaluation of content selection in generated explanations, via causal precision (is cited content actually part of a true reason?) and causal recall (is some complete reason covered?). Across four LLMs, end-to-end generation produces fluent explanations whose selected content rarely contradicts the input record yet is nonetheless about half irrelevant, at every model scale we test. The failure is content selection, not surface realization. Constraining length does not fix it. Under a one-sentence budget, models keep distractors and drop true reasons. Separating content determination from surface realization (an oracle selects content, the LLM only realizes it) restores near-perfect content precision and recall at equal fluency, and the guarantee survives audience adaptation into end-user and executive registers at a small realization cost. We release the benchmark, oracle, and evaluation suite.

paper.title: Decoding Path Recovery in Number Generation: Shifting to Intermediate Layers and Top-k Ranks

author.affiliation: School of Computer Science, University of Sheffield, Sheffield, UK
School of Computer Science, University of Sheffield, Sheffield, UK

paper.abstract: Existing work on numerical reasoning typically interprets incorrect outputs as failures of representation or computation. We instead study the recoverability of numerical errors: whether a correct answer remains accessible when considering a model’s intermediate layers or lower-ranked tokens despite an incorrect final output. Across eight open-source language models, we find that on average 30% of arithmetic failures remain recoverable beyond standard decoding, indicating that some numerical errors arise from selecting the wrong token rather than failing to compute it altogether. However, this recoverability is not universal. As arithmetic complexity increases, the correct answer progressively disappears not only from the model’s final prediction but also from alternative candidates and intermediate computations, revealing the limits of decoding-based recovery. Finally, we show that recoverable and unrecoverable failures exhibit distinct predictive dynamics with regard to probability and rank behaviour in intermediate layers, providing insight into when interventions such as adaptive decoding or post-generation correction are likely to succeed. Overall, our findings characterise both the opportunities and limitations of exploiting latent numerical information during generation.

paper.title: Cross-Lingual Activation Steering for Multilingual Language Models

author.affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Portland State University, USA
Department of Computer Science, Portland State University, USA
Carnegie Mellon University

paper.abstract: Large language models exhibit strong multilingual capabilities, yet significant performance gaps persist between dominant and non-dominant languages. Prior work attributes this gap to imbalances between shared and language-specific neurons in multilingual representations. We propose Cross-Lingual Activation Steering (CLAS), a training-free inference-time intervention that selectively modulates neuron activations. We evaluate CLAS on several multilingual downstream tasks and achieve improvements while maintaining high-resource language performance. We discover that effective transfer operates through functional divergence rather than strict alignment, and performance gains correlate with increased language cluster separation. Our results demonstrate that targeted activation steering can unlock latent multilingual capacity in existing models without modification to model weights.

paper.title: Beyond Natural Language Plans: Structure-Aware Agentic Planning for Query-Focused Table Summarization

author.affiliation: University of Amsterdam
ETH Zurich
Eindhoven University of Technology
University of Amsterdam

paper.abstract: Query-focused table summarization requires complex reasoning, often approached through step-by-step natural language (NL) plans. However, NL plans are inherently ambiguous and lack structure, making their conversion into executable programs like SQL brittle, especially for multi-table tasks. To address this, we introduce TaSoF, a schema-constrained, dependency-aware plan representation inspired by formalisms used in traditional multi-agent systems, and an agentic framework, SPaGe, that organizes the reasoning process into three phases: 1) Structured Planning to generate TaSoF from a query, 2) Graph-based Execution to convert plan steps into SQL and model dependencies via a directed acyclic graph for parallel execution, and 3) Summary Generation to produce query-focused summaries. Our method explicitly captures complex dependencies and supports dependency-aware execution. Experiments on two datasets show that SPaGe consistently outperforms prior models in the evaluated single- and multi-table settings and achieves higher per-step execution success than the evaluated NL plan formats.

paper.title: Clarify, Abstain or Answer? Strategising in Conversation with Belief-Augmented Generation

author.affiliation: University of Amsterdam
University of Amsterdam
MCML Munich; LMU Munich
European Commission, Joint Research Centre (JRC), Brussels; University of Amsterdam

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) define a distribution over text, which can be viewed as a probabilistic representation of uncertainty: sampling K responses yields a belief state— responses a model deems plausible. Existing work exploits this representation for narrow tasks like either decoding or selective prediction, and often requires manual interventions, not controlling generation directly. We propose Belief-Augmented Generation (BAG): grounding LLMs in their own belief state via the prompt and letting them reason over these K samples to decide on and execute a conversational strategy: clarify, abstain, or answer. In a multi-turn ambiguous question answering (QA) setting, we find that LLMs by default rarely clarify or abstain, ignoring uncertainty about the input (aleatoric) or facts (epistemic). BAG improves QA accuracy across six models and yields strategy decisions more faithful to their belief state than prompt-only baselines. Disentangling when to clarify from when to abstain, however, remains challenging.

paper.title: A Large-Scale Dataset for Cross-Lingual Multi-Jurisdiction Patent Drafting from Patent Cooperation Treaty Applications

author.affiliation: Kyoto Institute of Technology
Aichi Institute of Technology
Nagaoka Institute of Technology
Nara Women’s University
Kyoto Institute of Technology; RIKEN GRP

paper.abstract: Securing patent protection across countries requires drafting claims separately for each national patent office, in the relevant language and according to its legal and stylistic conventions. Patent claims can therefore differ across languages and jurisdictions because of translation, target-office drafting practices, and prosecution-stage changes. We formulate cross-lingual patent drafting as generating plausible candidate claim sets for a specified target language, jurisdiction, and prosecution stage from a source claim set in another language. The task models jurisdiction- and stage-specific transformations beyond content-preserving translation. We construct a large-scale Japanese–English dataset by linking Japan Patent Office (JPO) and United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) records through 884,179 Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT)-derived patent families. Across six released configurations, these families yield 4,067,168 directional claim-set instances; four core configurations form the main benchmark. paper.abstract: Fact-checking has had a tendency to overlook implicit claims, on which much misleading discourse depends. We propose a pipeline for detecting them based on the concept of the enthymeme, an argument with a missing component whose grounding in argumentation schemes allows implicit content to be recovered systematically. The pipeline proceeds in three steps: detecting whether a tweet contains enthymematic argumentation, generating the missing premise or conclusion, and assessing whether the reconstructed content constitutes a check-worthy claim. paper.abstract: LLM judges are increasingly used to evaluate generated text in multiple quality dimensions, where overall quality is implicitly built from fine-grained trait judgments. Across summarization, dialogue, and essay evaluation, we introduce a diagnostic framework that investigates the compositional relationship between overall and trait-level scores. We find that overall judgments are highly recoverable from traits (R2 = 0.675 to 0.945). However, this does not imply validity. Additionally, attribution methods agree with one another far more than any judge agrees with humans (Kendall’s τ = 0.47 to 1.00 internally vs. -0.07 to 0.20 against humans). An alignment diagnostic, computed at full sample size, localizes much of this gap to how traits are aggregated rather than how they are scored, and targeted perturbations show that correlational alignment overstates trait-level competence. Over multiple iterations across a set of frontier models, we compare three different approaches that estimate a model’s internal knowledge (as a form of LLM metacognition). First, multiple-choice questions are generated with the document to test models. Second, models must identify when no correct answer is present and generate a missing correct answer. Third, the models answers open-ended questions. Each approach tested models with and without document context. Experiments are conducted across multiple models on a corpus of technical and nontechnical Wikipedia articles sampled across revision periods relative to model training cutoffs. We present NexusEngine, which recasts document-to-twin conversion as ontology-constrained, provenance-grounded generation. Three ideas drive it: (i) visual-first conditioning that generates from layout rather than lossy text; (ii) schema-constrained multi-persona generation under a hard response schema; and (iii) a deterministic faithfulness stack (sanitiser, validator, fusion) with a bounded verify-and-repair loop, a bitemporal store, and a validation layer that ensures accepted deliveries. paper.abstract: Data-to-text driver coaching is often presented as a generic pipeline from telematics events to advice. This paper argues that its content requires localisation because usefulness and credibility depend on drivers’ knowledge, prevalent risks, regulation, infrastructure, and available data. The UK system prioritises post-trip reflection, explanations tied to road and place context, and tone-sensitive wording. paper.abstract: Lexical alignment, the tendency of interlocutors to adopt each other’s vocabulary during dialogue, is a phenomenon that contributes to mutual understanding, reduced cognitive load, and enhanced trust. Implementing controllable lexical alignment in dialogue systems, however, remains an open problem. Existing methods require user profiling or training data, and none provides continuous parametric control over the degree of alignment. We present a training-free, inference-time weighted decoding method that addresses these limitations. The method was evaluated with four architecturally diverse language models using 95 source dialogues from DailyDialog, resulting in 10,545 generated dialogues. These dialogues were assessed through a multi-judge LLM evaluation framework, complemented by a small scale human evaluation. The results show that weighted decoding provides effective, graded, and bidirectional control over lexical alignment across all evaluated model architectures, preserving generation quality within model-specific operating ranges that provide practical guidance for selecting appropriate weight factors.
