paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted in disaster risk management (DRM) for situational awareness tasks. An equally critical task is extracting and summarizing the underlying causes of a disaster for post-event reporting, which requires a higher-level of discourse comprehension. While pre-filtering the input data into “cause-specific” text seems to be a straightforward solution, cleaner inputs may not resolve all task-relevant issues. The limitations can stem from the LLMs’ core synthesis behaviors. To investigate this, we conduct a two-part study on multi-document summarization of flood causes. Part I investigates the impact of input granularity (document-level vs. sentence-level input). Part II evaluates how LLM-generated summaries differ from human-written summaries using a targeted funnel evaluation, conducting a multi-dimensional human annotation across more than 20 variables. Our findings reveal that while the sentence-level extraction step reduces non-causal content for smaller models, advanced and larger LLMs did not show significant reductions. Furthermore, while LLMs match humans in baseline relevance, deeper synthesis divergences persist. Structurally, LLM-generated summaries are longer and less coherent. Semantically, LLMs over-generate extreme descriptors and under-represent the more nuanced higher-level governmental responsibility.

paper.abstract: Scientific papers are long and technically dense, and frontier large language models can summarize them effectively, but their cost and API dependencies limit large-scale use. We distill scientific summarization from Claude Opus 4.6 into LLaMA 3.1 8B with LoRA and LLaMA 3.3 70B with QLoRA using 1,500 arXiv papers. On a 150-paper test set, the fine-tuned students improve BERTScore F1 against paper abstracts over zero-shot base models (p < 0.001; Cohen’s d up to 1.40 on the aggregate test set) and closely match the teacher’s abstractiveness profile, including novel trigram rate (∼77% vs. ∼64% for base) and extractive density (∼2.5 vs. ∼4.6). paper.abstract: The wide adoption of LLMs across broad NLG applications heightens the importance of providing users with the means to avert errors and hallucinations. Uncertainty quantification is poised to fill that gap; with low uncertainty (high confidence), as a proxy for correctness, allowing users to be selective (e.g., reject low-confidence, likely incorrect responses). Correlation between confidence and correctness then serves as a useful criterion for evaluation of uncertainty quantifiers (UQs). But in NLG, where diverse responses can be adequate to a prompt, obtaining reliable correctness judgements is not simple, especially without human intervention. Errors in automated judgement are hardly avoidable and known to diminish the reliability of evaluation protocols (Santilli et al., 2025; Ielanskyi et al., 2025). In a meta-analysis of published work, we show that automated judgement is the present norm. Besides, automated judgements are rarely validated against human ones, and the validation of the UQ evaluation they automate is even rarer. With experiments in question answering, using 4 LLMs, human and automated judgements and 7 popular UQs, we find that i) a judge’s performance can only coarsely predict the observed impact of its errors on the reliability of UQ evaluation, and that ii) judgement errors tend to misrepresent informative UQs most. We link these observations to patterns of correlation between confidence and categories of judgement error.

paper.abstract: Hybrid latent reasoning expands Large Language Models by replacing discrete text decoding with continuous “soft tokens,” yet it paradoxically falls behind text-space baselines such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on low-resource languages. paper.abstract: Oral exams can capture students’ conceptual understanding, but they are difficult to scale. To improve on scalability, this paper presents ACA-Bot, a speech-and-LLM-based oral examiner for introductory statistics. ACA-Bot uses a cascaded architecture combining speech recognition, LLM-based dialogue control, and text-to-speech, and is designed around pedagogical dimensions such as diagnostic questioning, adaptivity, neutrality, content alignment, coherence, consistency, and feedback quality. We evaluated the system through a user study, LLM-as-judge scoring, and qualitative conversation analysis. Results suggest that ACA-Bot is promising for formative assessment and exam preparation, particularly when pedagogical quality can be guided by prompts, rubrics, and predefined topic structures. The system performed less consistently on diagnostic and adaptive questioning, sometimes moving on before students had fully demonstrated their understanding. Speech-related problems, including interruptions and recognition errors, also affected interaction quality. These findings show the potential and limitations of spoken LLM-based assessment.

paper.title: The Truncation Blind Spot: How Decoding Strategies Systematically Exclude Human-Like Token Choices

author.affiliation: Department of Statistics, LMU Munich; Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML)

paper.abstract: Why does machine-generated text remain detectable? We investigate a mechanistic explanation at the decoding stage: standard strategies such as top-k and nucleus sampling restrict generation to high-probability tokens, while human writers routinely choose contextually appropriate words from deeper in the model’s probability distribution. Truncation makes a measurable share of these choices unreachable; we call this the truncation blind spot. Across five open models and three domains, 8–18% of human-selected tokens fall outside common truncation boundaries. Linguistic analysis further reveals disproportionate exclusion of content-word tokens. In a benchmark comprising 1.8 million machine generations, classifiers using only predictability and lexical diversity achieve mean AUC-ROC near 0.97, with substantial variation across decoding settings and strong transfer across generators. Probability-floor samplers substantially narrow the blind spot, demonstrating that the choice of truncation criterion matters for retaining human-used tokens. Together, these findings characterize a source of human–machine distributional mismatch and motivate decoding methods that preserve contextually appropriate low-probability choices while maintaining generation quality. Code and data are available at https://github.com/EstebanGarces/human_vs_machine.

paper.title: A Writer–Editor–Critic Pipeline with Deterministic Fact Verification for Football Match Report Generation

paper.abstract: Generating football match reports from structured data requires both factual accuracy and fluent prose: template-based systems favor accuracy, while large language models favor fluency but risk introducing unsupported content. We present a writer–editor–critic pipeline in which a writer verbalizes source triples as individual statements, an editor composes those statements into a report, and a critic uses an LLM to extract the report’s facts for deterministic comparison with the source triples. Precision, recall, F1, and a structured error report then drive a Reflexion-style loop for up to five rounds or until F1 reaches 100%. We compare atomic encoding, which represents each attribute as a separate triple, with hyper-relational encoding, which groups related attributes as qualifiers on a compound triple. On a dataset of 50 Liga Portugal matches, the loop converges for every article within four of the five allowed rounds, averaging 0.84 correction rounds for hyper-relational encoding and 1.12 for atomic encoding, with no unsupported content detected by this metric. Hyper-relational encoding reduces the mean triple count from 187 to 68 and the mean input payload from 3,195 to 1,853 tokens. CheckEval scores show positive associations with human preferences for fluency and naturalness, but not coherence. On a CheckEval-stratified diagnostic subset of 13 matches, annotators prefer reports generated from both representations over the deployed template baseline in at least 81% of comparisons; hyper-relational is preferred to atomic in 64% of coherence and naturalness comparisons.

paper.title: Token Distribution versus Data Volume: Domain Balancing in Multi-Domain Meeting Summarisation

paper.abstract: Jointly fine-tuning an LLM on meeting-summarisation corpora of widely varying size raises a question that prior work leaves confounded: when a domain-balanced training mixture helps, is the gain due to the distribution of tokens across domains, or merely to the volume of data seen? We disentangle these factors by constructing balanced and natural (native-proportional) token mixtures at matched token budgets (2-32M) over five English meeting corpora, fine-tuning Mistral-7B with QLoRA, and evaluating per domain. Balancing redistributes quality, improving the data-scarce minority domains at a low cost to the data-rich ones. The trade favours balancing whenever the minority domains matter: their share under proportional allocation is fixed at 1-2% regardless of budget, so matching balanced quality on those domains requires far more total data. We further find that pruning low-value transcript lines removes ∼15% of tokens from the conversational corpora at no measurable cost, and that balancing by tokens is not the same as balancing by examples. Fine-tuning one model per domain is competitive only on the data-rich domains and falls below the zero-shot model on the data-scarce ones. A two-annotator study of 741 judge-labelled facts validates our fact-level evaluation. Together these results give practitioners a basis for deciding when to balance an imbalanced multi-domain mixture, and on what unit.

paper.abstract: Large language models can produce fluent clinical summaries whose most dangerous errors are often omissions: clinically relevant facts may disappear without creating an explicit contradiction. In privacy-constrained hospital settings, an omission detector must run on-premise, require no gold summary, and avoid additional large language model calls for evaluation. We reproduce and stress-test EmbedKDECheck, a source-grounded, reference-free embedding-density detector, on a controlled French medical corpus in which summaries are generated from source variants with known fact-deletion rates across sixteen graded levels. We adapt the published pipeline to this graded setting with a bounded mean-based score, and replace principal component analysis with a random projection. The resulting configuration improves all reported held-out metrics while reducing the dimensionality-reduction cost, reaching a Spearman correlation of 0.48, F1 of 0.80 on complete-versus-half-omitted summaries, and roughly 573 thousand floating-point operations per document pair. We then characterise the main remaining limitation: a report-specific score offset that explains most score variance and limits corpus-level rank correlation. Targeted follow-up interventions show that this offset is removable only with anchor summaries that violate the frugality constraint. Overall, the simple static-embedding and random-projection pipeline offers a frugal operating point for source-grounded completeness evaluation, lying on the graded rank-correlation/cost frontier among non-LLM and mid-cost reference-free metrics.

paper.abstract: Choosing a Natural Language Generation (NLG) pipeline is difficult when the generated output must be functionally correct, measurably effective, and inexpensive to produce, all at once. We propose an evaluation framework for comparing NLG pipelines under these joint constraints, together with the Inference-Adjusted Gain (IAG), an architecture-agnostic metric combining output quality and inference cost. We instantiate the framework on energy-aware code refactoring: five systems (LLM-only, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Knowledge-Augmented Generation (KAG), Agentic RAG, and Token-Efficient Agentic RAG (TeaRAG)) share the same 1,368-entry knowledge base (KB), named GreenKB, backbone LLM, and validation protocol across 11 Python programs, including three real GitHub projects. Only TeaRAG passes the functional gate on all three GitHub projects, with confirmed energy reductions on two; the third remains within measurement noise. Every other system passes at most one project. A rollback ablation traces this robustness mainly to orchestration rather than retrieval alone. On three synthetic scripts, each run over five seeds, TeaRAG again achieves the highest IAG: it cuts energy use by 96 % on average, against 88 % for KAG, at a higher token cost (3.6k vs. 2.2k tokens). One synthetic case is unstable across seeds for every system, leaving the margin over KAG narrow.

paper.title: Confabulation in a Caption-then-Generate Pipeline: Evaluating Vision–Language Generation of Adolescent Health Information

author.affiliation: School of Health and Human Performance, Dublin City University, Ireland

paper.abstract: Vision-language models make it newly possible to turn a photograph into written health information, but producing text an adolescent can act on is harder than producing text that is merely fluent. We evaluate an off-the-shelf pipeline for this task, in which Florence-2-Large captions an image and Llama 3 8B Instruct generates a health message from that caption. Applying it to images taken by adolescents during a school Photovoice session, a participatory method in which young people photograph their own surroundings, we then collect ratings from six health-literacy evaluators on clarity, relevance, and helpfulness. Comparing each narrative with its caption, we find that many assert content the caption never contained, a behaviour we call confabulation, and that its severity tracks how unhelpful evaluators judged the output to be. Judging only the outputs, the evaluators independently identified three recurring gaps, which map onto three recognised challenges in natural language generation. Our findings show why fluent output is not the same as usable output, and why domain-expert evaluation is needed to tell them apart.

paper.title: Reference-Based Analysis of Coherence and Diversity in Open-Ended Text Generation

author.affiliation: Department of Statistics, LMU Munich; Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML)

paper.abstract: Evaluating open-ended text generation involves understanding how different properties of a continuation relate to its perceived quality. We present a reference-based framework for examining coherence and diversity through three perspectives: aligning their evolution with human trajectories, comparing their summaries with a human continuation of the same prompt, and estimating their likelihood under a human reference distribution. Experiments with human quality ratings suggest that diversity-based alignment and mean-based comparisons capture quality-related variation, although the comparisons do not establish a predictive advantage for temporal alignment over simpler baselines. Reference likelihood also shows positive associations with ratings, with results varying across reference configurations and scoring horizons. Together, these analyses provide a structured way to examine how measured coherence and diversity relate to human judgments, while distinguishing similarity to human references from quality itself. Code and analysis resources are available at https://github.com/EstebanGarces/likely_human.

paper.title: You Can’t Prefer Emotions You Don’t Sample: Intensity Undershoot in DPO-Tuned LLMs

author.affiliation: Independent

paper.abstract: Ask a language model to respond “very excitedly,” and its output is typically only mildly more energetic. We quantify this effect. We condition an instruction-tuned LLM on a continuous Valence–Arousal (VA) target (Russell, 1980), where valence measures how pleasant a state is and arousal how activated it is, measure the achieved affect with a frozen regressor, and sweep the requested target from −1 to +1. The response moves far less than asked: the gain, the slope of achieved against requested affect, is only 0.26 for valence and 0.13 for arousal on Llama-3.1-8B, where a faithful controller would score 1. The model systematically undershoots requested emotional intensity, which puts a number on the qualitative observation of Fazzi et al. (2025). Our experiments trace this to the preference-learning pipeline. Training targets from natural corpora such as EmoBank are neutral-heavy, and the sampled candidates themselves rarely reach extreme affect, so Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is left with no extreme exemplar to prefer. If instead we cover the target space uniformly and sample a hotter, larger candidate pool, valence gain rises from 0.26 to 0.40 ± 0.02 (3 seeds) and extrapolation error drops, at only a modest in-distribution cost (EmoBank-test VA distance 0.092 → 0.107). The same recipe reproduces on Qwen3-8B (gain 0.44, with in-distribution accuracy preserved). Arousal is harder and less reliable: its gain barely moves on average and swings across seeds (0.14 ± 0.07, against valence’s tight ±0.02), because raising arousal needs candidates the base model is reluctant to generate. The evidence indicates that faithful intensity is bottlenecked by the extremity of the candidate pool rather than by the conditioning format.

paper.title: Example-Guided Prompting for Document-Level Text Simplification

paper.abstract: Document-level text simplification requires large language models (LLMs) to rewrite complex documents while preserving meaning, readability, and discourse coherence. Although prompt-based LLMs have shown promising performance, they often produce inconsistent simplifications because textual instructions alone provide limited guidance for complex document-level transformations. We investigate whether retrieved document-simplification examples can improve document-level generation by augmenting prompts with examples selected from a parallel simplification corpus. This example-guided prompting approach enables LLMs to exploit relevant simplification patterns without task-specific fine-tuning. Experiments on the OneStopEnglish corpus using multiple state-of-the-art LLMs show that incorporating retrieved examples generally improves simplification quality over prompt-only generation and achieves competitive or superior performance compared with representative supervised (T5) and planning-based (PlanSimp) document simplification systems. Furthermore, we find that the benefits of example-guided prompting vary across LLMs, suggesting that effective use of retrieved examples depends on a model’s ability to integrate contextual information during generation.

paper.title: Sleight of Word Benchmark: Can Language Models Notice If Their Own Output Was Tampered With?

author.affiliation: Cleo

paper.abstract: The output of a Language Model can be tampered with while the model is writing it. A simple test can thus be constructed by evaluating the model’s perception of this external perturbation. In this spirit, a simple benchmark is built in which a single word is consistently substituted with another in the generation process. We call this method Sleight of Word. Two distinct axes are measured: metrics that relate to the model’s surprise, as well as an evaluation of the textual reaction for 19 different open-weight language models.

paper.title: The Impact of Model Size on Detection of LLM Hallucinations

author.affiliation: University of Amsterdam
University of Amsterdam

paper.abstract: Large Language Models have radically improved the capabilities of natural language generation. However, LLMs may generate hallucinations. To begin to tackle this challenge, work has emerged on hallucination detection. Currently, hallucination detectors are often compared across models that differ simultaneously in size, architecture, and adaptation, making it unclear where performance derives from. In particular, the role of model size is underexplored where having small models may be beneficial in application settings. To address this gap, we systematically investigate hallucination detection across four open-weight model families spanning encoder-based natural language inference, sequence-to-sequence instruction following, and decoder-only instruction models. Within each family, we evaluate multiple parameter scales both out of the box and after task-specific training. Out-of-the-box scaling is strongly architecture-dependent. After training, size-performance relationships become more consistently positive across all four families. On the SHROOM hallucination detection benchmark, Qwen-7B achieves the strongest overall result, with 0.845 accuracy, while substantially smaller DeBERTa models remain competitive. These results show that parameter count alone is an incomplete basis for selecting hallucination detectors: the benefits of scaling depend on architecture and task-specific adaptation.

paper.title: Assessing Legal Argumentation in Generated Judgments: A Toulmin-Based Evaluation Framework

author.affiliation: Department of Information and Computing Sciences, Utrecht University, the Netherlands

paper.abstract: Legal judgments require sound legal reasoning in order for justice to occur. Existing work on automated judgment prediction has largely focused on predicting the final decision, while ignoring the quality of the underlying legal argumentation. Existing semantic similarity metrics evaluate the semantic similarity of generated texts, but it remains unclear whether they reflect the legal correctness of judicial reasoning. This paper makes two contributions: first, a novel framework for evaluating the legal argumentation of generated judgments based on Toulmin models; second, an application of this framework to a set of generated judgments of appellate negligence cases, and a comparison with contemporary semantic similarity metrics. Our results show that, despite achieving competitive performance on outcome prediction, the evaluated model frequently produces legally deficient reasoning. Moreover, we find that contemporary semantic similarity metrics do not capture the same judicial argumentation qualities as our framework.

paper.abstract: Direct Speech-to-Text Translation (DS2TT) generates target language text directly from source speech without requiring intermediate source language transcriptions. However, developing DS2TT for low resource, scriptless tribal languages is challenging due to limited parallel data. We investigate heterographic transcriptions as auxiliary supervision in DS2TT for four Indian tribal languages: Lambani, Soliga, Kui, and Mundari. We evaluate three transcription strategies: contact language scripts, contact language influenced IPA, and HuBERT based pseudo text. Using parallel corpora of speech, heterographic transcriptions, and English translations, we train DS2TT models with cross modal learning. Results show that heterographic transcriptions significantly improve translation quality over speech only baselines, while inference remains transcription free, requiring only speech input.

paper.abstract: We present SAGE (Semantic Abstraction Generation from Events), a modular data-to-text pipeline that converts continuous Age of Empires II (AoE2) game-state snapshots and events into live text commentary updates, pairing rule-based content selection with a large language model (LLM) realizer. Its content selection operationalizes how human commentators forage the game for information through two independently ablatable strategies: Expert Insights (strategic context) and Event Structuring (grouping parallel events). Alongside the pipeline we release its underlying corpus: continuous full game-state snapshots for 3,100 ladder and 176 tournament AoE2 matches (142 with paired professional commentary video), to our knowledge the first full-state corpus for a complex esports title. We also report on a preliminary user study with 33 AoE2 viewers.

paper.abstract: The field of natural language generation (NLG) is naturally quite quantitative in nature and mindset. However, quantitative methodologies can give us measures but not tell us what to measure or why it matters. Here we document our efforts to conduct a qualitative study of changing evaluation practices in NLG-adjacent research communities. We share our experience designing a semi-structured interview procedure, the kinds of conversations that result, how they differ from our expectations as NLP researchers, and where we are going next in our study, along with early insights from the initial coding of interview transcripts.

paper.abstract: Reading comprehension is often assessed with multiple-choice questions (MCQs). This paper leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) for automatic generation of distractors for MCQs, and for automatic evaluation of distractor plausibility. We show that fine-tuning an LLM on a modest-sized dataset can lead to automatically generated distractors that rival human-crafted ones in plausibility. Further, we analyze how LLMs differ from humans in making judgments on distractor plausibility.

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are prone to hallucinating or misinterpreting facts, which impairs their usability in retrieval-augmented generation or data-to-text systems. We analyse how faithfulness of LLMs to provided context depends on how plausible they perceive the context to be (context–memory conflict). To better identify error patterns, we make use of the increased difficulty of non-English and low-resource language text generation and input data based on local knowledge, only partially captured in models’ parametric knowledge. We let the models generate text in English, Czech, Slovak and Upper Sorbian from factual (FA), counterfactual (CFA) and fictional (FI) RDF triples containing local Czech and Slovak data. Contrary to our expectations, we observe only a weak context–memory conflict on the human-annotated sample. For Kimi K3 as an LLM judge, which agrees well with human annotations on the sample, counterfactual inputs receive only slightly lower faithfulness scores than factual ones (−0.05 on a 1–5 scale). We also find that a suboptimal choice of LLM judge would lead to overestimating the strength of the context–memory conflict.

paper.abstract: Current evaluation of metaphor explanations relies mainly on holistic quality ratings, revealing little about how explanation quality is structured or where human judgments agree and diverge. We introduce a cognitively motivated framework that decomposes metaphor explanation quality into six theoretically grounded dimensions. In a dense annotation study (11,200 ratings), we find that: (i) explanation quality is genuinely multidimensional; (ii) annotator disagreement is systematic rather than random; and (iii) the six dimensions collapse into a shared cluster and two independent axes of judgment. An exploratory feasibility study further shows that a standard automatic evaluation pipeline can recover parts of this structure, predicting the most discriminative dimensions well while its errors correlate human (dis)agreement. Together, these results suggest that multidimensional evaluation offers richer diagnostic insight than holistic ratings, and that automatic evaluators for open-ended generation tasks should be judged on how well they preserve the structure of human judgment.

paper.abstract: Data augmentation via LLM paraphrases is an appealing way to expand scarce training data for aspect-based tasks in low-resource languages. We test whether it helps on the Portuguese ABSAPT 2024 benchmark, using PTT5 as the target model. A simple PTT5 baseline already surpasses the best shared-task systems on both sub-tasks. We then augment training with paraphrases from two LLM families (Qwen2.5-7B and Gemma-3-Gaia-4B), generated at a high temperature with an anchoring prompt and selected by an explicit diversity filter based on low similarity to the source while preserving every aspect term verbatim. Although the retained paraphrases are measurably diverse and aspect-faithful by construction, augmentation yields no gain: aspect extraction consistently degrades across five seeds and both LLMs, while sentiment classification changes remain within seed variability. We characterise the generated data along semantic and surface-form axes and show that the injected diversity is predominantly lexical: the paraphrases move the training distribution away from the test set without providing evidence of additional semantic coverage beyond that of the human data.

paper.abstract: Hate detection in memes involves an inherent trade-off between over-detection, which may suppress legitimate expression, and under-detection, which may allow harmful content to spread. Therefore, beyond improving detection accuracy, it is important to make the decision-making process transparent and assess the quality of its underlying reasoning. In this study, we extend REPS, a reasoning-enhancement framework, to the multimodal setting in order to improve both the explainability and detection sensitivity of vision–language models for context-dependent hateful meme detection. Our approach enables the model to iteratively select and learn from self-generated rationales. Experimental results show that explanation plausibility improves with an approximately 60% win rate while achieving a recall of 0.960. These findings demonstrate that reasoning-enhanced multimodal learning improves both explanation quality and detection sensitivity, while highlighting the trade-off introduced by over-reasoning.

paper.abstract: Large language models routinely produce fluent output that is factually wrong or unsupported by the provided source, yet the neurons responsible for this behaviour remain poorly understood outside English. We present CAP (Contrastive Activation Patching), an open-source toolkit that locates, compares, and steers the neurons a model uses for a target behaviour across languages. From two contrastive groups of inputs, one command-line invocation captures per-neuron activations, ranks them with a Welch t-test and Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction, and patches them to measure their causal effect on a benchmark; the same signal doubles as a training-free steering rule, and interactive viewers support per-layer inspection and cross-language comparison.

paper.abstract: Disagreement in contested domains often reflects different assumptions and reasoning norms rather than simple factual errors. We present TruthSplit, a system that generates unified multi-perspective reasoning graphs for contested claims. The resulting TruthPath representation encodes shared premises and assumptions, typed divergence points, perspective-specific reasoning paths, and final stances, and combines an interactive visualization with a textual meta-analysis. An expert evaluation of generated TruthPaths provides initial evidence of analytical quality, while a user study with 22 participants indicates that the interface supports identifying shared ground and sources of disagreement. TruthSplit provides an inspectable representation of how different assumptions and values can lead to different conclusions without adjudicating which perspective is correct.

paper.abstract: This paper presents a tool for interactive digitisation of documents using Irish Gaelic script. The system, SeanchlÓCR, uses a transformer-based OCR model fine-tuned through an iterative refinement process. In addition to achieving lower character error rate than any other currently available system, our proposed framework also provides users with adjusted confidence scores for each word transcribed, allowing users to locate transcription errors and perform post-editing. The framework allows multiple users to post-edit concurrently and integrates semantic search, enabling users to retrieve previously digitised documents. It is hoped that the system can accelerate digitisation of important cultural artifacts by providing an effective transcription, search and post-editing framework.
